_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [livescience.com] Swallowable paper battery powers medical devices in pigs
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers developed a small battery made from magnesium and molybdenum trioxide that can be swallowed to power temporary medical devices inside the gastrointestinal tract. In pig tests, the battery produced a peak voltage of 1.84 volts and operated for up to three days, powering a wireless throat tag that transmitted to a receiver 1.5 metres away and a capsule that electrically stimulated the stomach for 20 minutes [scimex.org#1][livescience.com#1]. The battery uses materials intended to break down in the body after use, potentially removing the need to retrieve conventional batteries from temporary ingestible devices. The study remains at an early animal-testing stage: researchers tested a small number of pigs, and the circuit board did not fully degrade but passed in the animals' feces [scimex.org#1]. MIT said the researchers built two versions—a 7.5-millimetre disc and a 24-millimetre rectangular bar—for possible drug-delivery, sensing and other applications [mit.edu#1].

items.title: [npr.org] El Niño fuels Pacific storms as Atlantic lacks hurricanes
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An exceptionally strong El Niño is driving sharply different hurricane seasons in the Pacific and Atlantic. By Sept. 25, the Pacific had recorded 41 named storms, including 18 hurricanes, while the Atlantic had produced no hurricanes [npr.org#1]. Scientists cited El Niño as a key reason for the contrast [npr.org#1][abcnews.com#1]. Hurricane Polo rapidly intensified off Mexico, while Hurricane Nolo strengthened south of Hawaii. Nolo threatened the Big Island with extreme rain, flash flooding and mudslides. Forecasts called for 15 to 30 inches of rain in parts of the Big Island, with higher local totals possible; Nolo was not expected to make landfall [nasa.gov#1][earthsky.org#1][gpb.org#1][koaa.com#1].
